Consequently, the IQ-denial and blank slateism factors were deemed the most unique, relative to the other factors. We therefore removed these two factors and their associated indicators but kept all items belonging to the other scales. We then reran the same analyses with the same three model specifications but with 14 first-order factors instead of 16, on a total of 64 indicators instead of 70, to obtain estimates based on a model with better fit to its 1 Lavaan's computation of robust fit indices (CFI, TLI, and RMSEA) failed for the bifactor model in the first round of analyses. Manual calculations based on the scaled χ 2 for the baseline and test model, resulted in a CFI identical to the non-robust version and a robust RMSEA that was implausibly small. For the revised models, computation of robust absolute fit indices succeeded for all three models. Consequently, we report both robust and non-robust absolute fit indices for these analyses, but we stick to non-robust indices when directly comparing with model fit estimates from the first round.

data matrix. Removing these two factors resulted in more well-fitting modelsfoot_0 , particularly for CFI, as shown in Table 1.

Weak Generality (Hypothesis 1)

The ESEM with target rotation yielded excellent fit: χ 2 (1067) = 1414 (p < .001), CFI robust = .993, RMSEA robust = .012[.010, .014]. The mean latent correlation between the primary factors in the revised correlated factors model dropped from .62 in the independent clusters model CFA (ICM-CFA) to .39 in the ESEM with target rotation, indicating that the correlations were inflated in CFA due to unmodeled cross-loadings. Latent correlations based on both CFA and ESEM are reported in Figure 1. The smallest latent correlations based on the CFA are in the lower .4 range, with most considerably higher. In the ESEM, the correlations between conspiracy mentality and astrology, as well as climate change denial and financial conspiracism, dropped enough to become insignificant. Nevertheless, most correlations remained highly significant and substantially correlated. Even in the ESEM, 57 out of 91 correlations (i.e., 62.6%) were strong (≥ .30) and only 6 (i.e., 6.6%) were weak (< .20). Heatmap of Latent Correlations between Factors Note. Estimates based on the correlated factors ICM-CFA model are in the lower diagonal and estimates from ESEM with target rotation are in the upper diagonal. The ω t reliabilities are presented in the diagonal, with standardized loadings of first-order factors on the secondorder factor (in parentheses) in the column and row names.

Strong Generality (Hypothesis 2)

The correlated factors model clearly evinced better model fit than its competitors, contrary to the strong generality hypothesis (see Table 1). On the other hand, the bifactor model and, to a lesser extent, the second-order model also fit the data reasonably well, at least according to RMSEA. The ECV and ω h of the general factor in the bifactor model were .61, suggesting that 61% of the variance accounted for by the latent factors was attributable to the general factor. Taken together, these results provide weak or partial support for a strong generality.

Conspiratorial vs. Non-Conspiratorial Content (Hypothesis 3)

As can be gleaned from Figure 1, the factors representing conspiratorial content tend to show higher correlations between themselves, compared to the correlations with nonconspiratorial factors, and vice versa. Furthermore, the patterns of correlations between nonconspiratorial factors are generally smaller (although still large in absolute terms) compared to the correlations between the conspiratorial factors, suggesting that the non-conspiratorial factors have less overlap and more uniqueness relative to each other.

The model with two correlated second-order factors, χ 2 (1754) = 7153 (p < .001), CFI robust = .906, TLI robust = .902, RMSEA robust = .049[.047, .051], displayed marginally better model fit compared to the second-order model (Table 1), which is its nested counterpart: Δχ²(1) = 180 (p < .001), ΔCFI robust = .002; ΔRMSEA robust = .001. The latent correlation between the two second-order factors was ρ = .89, which explains the very small change in model fit.

Taken together, the very high correlation between the two factors and the minor change in model fit when formally separating the conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial clusters of beliefs indicates that there is little statistical distinction between conspiratorial and nonconspiratorial content in these data, contrary to Hypothesis 3.

Ideological Tilt (Hypothesis 4)

As can be observed in Figure 1, the factors representing left-wing misinformation show higher correlations between themselves, compared to correlations with factors representing right-wing and neutral forms of misinformation; and the same is in most cases true for the factors representing right-wing forms of misinformation. A second-order model dividing up the first-order factors into three correlated second-order factors, each representing rightaligned, left-aligned, and ideologically neutral misinformation, χ 2 (1693) = 6268 (p < .001), CFI robust = .917, TLI robust = .913, RMSEA robust = .047[0.45, 0.48], displayed significantly better model fit than the model with the conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial divide: Δχ²(2) = 492(p < .001), ΔCFI robust =.011, ΔRMSEA robust = .002, as well as the model with only one secondorder factor: Δχ²(3) = 880(p < .001), ΔCFI robust =.013, ΔRMSEA robust = .003. This indicates support for Hypothesis 4.

Discussion

The results provide clear support for a weaker version of the generality hypothesis (Bensley et al., 2020 (Bensley et al., , 2022)). Although the correlations between the factors dropped considerably in ESEM, the majority remained large (≥ .30) and almost all remained significant. Furthermore, the results provide partial support for the strong generality hypothesis, which posits that a general factor adequately accounts for individual differences in misinformation susceptibility. On the one hand, the two models containing a general factor yielded decent indices of absolute fit (RMSEA). The bifactor model in particular showed adequate fit based on CFI, even though the fitting propensity of bifactor models is inversely correlated with the number of specific factors (Bonifay et al., 2025). On the other hand, the correlated factors model showed substantially better model fit than the second-order and bifactor models, especially in terms of the incremental fit indices like CFI. Finally, the ECV of the general factor was .61, which means that while the general factor accounted for over half of the common variance among the latent factors, it was clearly short of what would be expected of a dominant general factor (e.g., ECV > .7-.8).

As to whether common sources of variance for non-conspiratorial vis-à-vis conspiratorial content are best modeled as separate or as one factor, we found that the fit of a model with two correlated second-order factors improved little in absolute terms, compared to its nested equivalent containing only one second-order factor. The small change in model fit could be explained by a latent correlation between the two second-order factors of r = .89. Shi et al. (2018, p. 679) proposed that "the misfit corresponding to ρ = 0.90 [between factors with independent clusters] is substantively ignorable" in the sense of being large enough that opting for a one-factor model makes sense for the purpose of parsimony. Accordingly, these results could be interpreted as failing to support a meaningful, statistical distinction between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial misinformation susceptibility. Nevertheless, the sheer size of the model still means that there are large amounts of unmodeled cross-loadings that likely greatly inflated the latent correlation between the two higher-order factors. This should invite caution in interpreting these results too strongly.

By contrast, dividing up the first-order factors between three second-order factors representing hypothesized ideological alignment of item content (right-wing, left-wing, neutral) resulted in significant and marked improvements in model fit relative to the other two second-order models, particularly in terms of the incremental fit indices. This suggests that the ideological tilt of the misinformation could account for systematic (co)variances in the data better than the rival models.

Another result worth noting is that initial analyses suggested that the factors representing misinformed beliefs about the effects of genes (blank slateism) and IQ yielded poor model fit. In other words, endorsement of these beliefs seemed to represent something relatively unique compared to the other measures included.

Finally, the CFA-based factor correlations between general conspiracy mentality and specific conspiracy theories were generally at least as large as those between the specific conspiracy theories. Furthermore, these correlations dropped considerably relative to the other factors in the ESEM and the factor loading matrix showed relatively small primary loadings and relatively large secondary loadings for the conspiracy mentality factor, suggesting that there was difficulty differentiating this factor from the others. In other words, it may function more as a general factor than as a unique, correlated factor alongside the others. This pattern is consistent with previous literature describing conspiracy mentality as a generalized disposition, worldview, or political attitude (Imhoff & Bruder, 2014; Nera, 2024), reflecting core ingredients of conspiratorial thinking, such as anti-authority or anti-establishment stances (Imhoff, 2024).

Limitations

An important cause for concern is the possibility that careless or overly consistent responding created spuriously high covariances in the data (Baumgartner & Steenkamp, 2001) inflated by common method variance (Spector et al., 2017). Biases in response styles on behalf of participants could well result in systematic method covariance in the data (e.g., Podsakoff et al., 2003 Podsakoff et al., , 2012)), which becomes indistinguishable from systematic substantive covariance. In addition, the scales typically exhibited a positively skewed distribution, which means that it is possible that for example inattentive responses could inflate correlations between them (i.e., systematically producing scores above the mean).

Study 2

This study replicated and extended the first study in a British quota sample. The survey included the same scales as in the first study, except that two items measuring belief in paranormal phenomena (categorized as ideologically neutral misinformation) were added. We shortened a few of the scales to reduce the response burden on participants without requiring planned missingness. Furthermore, the survey contained a subset of items unrelated to the study's focal constructs (i.e., a "marker variable", Williams et al., 2010), which allowed us to test the degree to which the measures were contaminated by method variance (Maydeu-Olivares & Steenkamp, 2025) producing spuriously high correlations. Insofar as the marker variable and the constructs of interests are theoretically unrelated, any correlation between them should reflect only common method variance.

Methods

Participants

A total of 3053 British adults were recruited through Prolific, as the first wave of a larger, longitudinal research project. Sample size was determined by availability of resources and power calculations for future longitudinal analyses, with expected rates of attrition taken into account.

The sample was stratified to contain an equal number of individual with/without higher education and the proportions of individuals in three age categories (18-34, 35-49, 50+) were calibrated against UK census data within both education strata. This was done because the UK participant pool on Prolific deviates greatly from the general population in terms of age and education (i.e., the young and highly educated are heavily overrepresented), and both these demographic characteristics are associated with susceptibility to misinformation (e.g., Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2024; Nilsson et al., 2019; Sultan et al., 2024). The participants completed a Qualtrics-survey. Those who failed more than one out of three attention checks, completed the survey in less than a fourth of the median sample response time, or only completed initial parts of the survey were excluded, leaving 3005 participants (M age = 43.3; SD age = 13.6; 55% women, 43% men; 76% with some form of post-secondary education and 23% with an upper secondary school degree or equivalent as highest level of education).

Measures

The participants responded to all items except for the bullshit items on 7-point Likert scales ranging from 1 ("Definitely false") to 7 ("Definitely true"). Several scales were shortened, and in a handful of cases, items were substituted (for full list of measures, see supplemental documents). Reliability estimates for the scales are presented in Figure 2. New for this study were two items measuring belief in the paranormal (e.g., "It is possible in some cases to make contact with the dead"; Nilsson & Bäckström, 2024) and three items measuring attitude to the color blue (e.g., "Blue is a lovely color"; Miller & Simmering, 2023) used as a marker variable.

Statistical Analyses

The same statistical analyses as in Study 1 were run. However, all models failed to converge when treating general conspiracy mentality and belief in conspiracy theories about sham democracy as separate factors-and the latent correlation between these factors was as high as .99 when we manually inspected the Φ-matrix of a correlated factors model that failed to converge. Consequently, the two scales were collapsed into a general conspiracism factor in all models, which consistently resolved the estimation issues. The model with two correlated second-order factors still resulted in non-convergence and a Heywood-case, however. Inspection of the ϴ-matrix revealed that the first indicator for the climate change denial factor had a negative residual (with a standardised factor loading of λ = .97). We constrained the residual variance of this item to the same small yet positive, estimated value in the model with only one second-order factor, which converged successfully. To be able to compare this model to the other second-order factor models (i.e., to make the models nested), we applied the same constraint to the residual of the same item for all the second-order models involved in testing Hypotheses 2, 3, and 4.

Furthermore, there were some issues related to the information matrix of the fully orthogonally specified bifactor model (for more details, see supplementary materials). Rather than report (misleadingly good) fit indices for a bifactor model where specific factors are allowed to covary, we chose to focus on the second-order model as representing a common factor model in this study. We did use the factor loading matrix and residual (co)variance matrix of a successfully converged orthogonal bifactor model solely for the purpose of calculating ECV and ω h for this study as well.

To investigate common method covariance across scales, we ran zero-order bivariate correlations between the index scores of the marker variable and the substantive constructs of interest, reporting Spearman's rho due to the skewness (-.099) of the marker variable.

As some factors had only two indicators in this study, Principal Axis Factoring instead of CFA was used for deriving the Omega-total coefficient for these factors.

Results

A second-order factor model containing IQ-denial and blank-slateism among the primary factors was first run: χ 2 (1579) = 14307 (p < .001), CFI robust = .859, TLI robust = .852, RMSEA robust = .056[0.55, 0.57]. Both had very low loadings on the second-order factor relative to the other factors: λ = .14 for IQ-denial and λ = .22 for blank slateism-that is, they once again exhibited high amounts of uniqueness. We therefore excluded them from the primary analyses like we did in Study 1.

Weak Generality (Hypothesis 1)

The correlated factors models displayed adequate fit once again: χ 2 (1183) = 6287 (p < .001), CFI robust = .941, TLI robust = .933, RMSEA robust = .041[0.40, 0.42]. ESEM with target rotation yielded further improvements in fit: χ 2 (689) = 1410 (p < .001), CFI robust = .991, TLI robust = .983, RMSEA robust = .019[0.17, 0.20]. The mean latent correlation dropped from .42 in the CFA model to .31 in the ESEM, suggesting that the latent correlations based on the ICM-CFA were to some extent spuriously high in this study too. The latent correlations between the factors estimated both through CFA and ESEM are presented in Figure 2.

Although seven latent correlations (i.e., 7.7% of the total) were rendered insignificant in the ESEM, 45 out 91 (i.e., 49.5%) remained strong (≥ .30) while 24 (i.e., 26.4%) were weak (< .20). In other words, the latent correlations were generally somewhat lower compared to Study 1 but still substantial and significant in most cases. The highest average latent correlations emerged for some of the factors with conspiratorial content (e.g., general conspiracism, political correctness, and alien coverup; r mean ≥ .38) while the lowest emerged for financial and anti-west conspiracy theories as well as all non-conspiratorial scales except for pseudoscience belief (r mean ≤ .26). Heatmap of Latent Correlations between Factors Note. Estimates based on the correlated factors ICM-CFA model are in the lower diagonal and estimates from ESEM with target rotation are in the upper diagonal. Reliabilities are presented in the diagonal, with standardized loadings of first-order factors on the second-order factor (in parentheses) in the column and row names.

Strong Generality (Hypothesis 2)

The model with a second-order factor explaining the covariance between the specific factors resulted in poor model fit: χ 2 (1261) = 12522 (p < .001), CFI robust = .869, TLI robust = .862, RMSEA robust = .059[0.58, 0.60]. Furthermore, the ECV and ω h of the general factor based on a confirmatory bifactor model was .47, suggesting that the general factor accounted for less than half the common variance among latent factors. Consequently, there was no clear support for strong generality.

Conspiratorial vs. non-conspiratorial content (Hypothesis 3)

The factors representing scales with conspiratorial content once again showed slightly higher correlations between themselves on average, compared to the correlations with nonconspiratorial factors, and vice versa (see Figure 2). An exception was that climate change denial correlated more strongly with the conspiratorial factors than with the other nonconspiratorial ones, and both bullshit receptivity and belief in conspiracy theories about aliens correlated equally strongly with other factors in both groups. The correlations between the non-conspiratorial factors were also somewhat smaller on average, suggesting that these scales (particularly climate change denial and bullshit receptivity) captured more unique variation in this study as well.

The model with two second-order factors, χ 2 (1260) = 11365 (p < .001), CFI robust = .883, TLI robust = .876, RMSEA robust = .056[0.55, 0.57], exhibited better fit; Δχ²(1) = 1904 (p < .001), χ 2 (1260) = 11362 (p < .001), ΔCFI robust = .014, ΔTLI robust = .014, ΔRMSEA robust = .003, compared to its nested counterpart with one general second-order factor. The latent correlation between the two second-order factors was r = .67, which is considerably smaller compared to the first study, but still indicates considerable overlap between conspiratorial and nonconspiratorial misinformation susceptibility 3.

Ideological content (Hypothesis 4)

The correlation matrix for the correlated factors model shows that there were indeed particularly strong correlations between factors representing right-wing misinformation (great

Given the substandard model fit, this latent correlation is likely to reflect an overestimate due to unmodeled cross-loadings, as was the case in the first study.

replacement, political correctness, reverse discrimination, and global warming denial) as well as some of the scales representing left-wing misinformation (financial and anti-west conspiracies) and neutral misinformation (pseudoscience, paranormal beliefs, and conspiracy theories about aliens). On the other hand, the conspiracy theory factors classified as ideologically neutral (general conspiracism, antisemitic conspiracies, and alien coverup) also showed high correlations with some of the ideologically tilted conspiracy belief factors (see

Figure 2).

The model with three second-order factors representing left-wing, neutral, and rightwing content, χ 2 (1258) = 10722 (p < .001), CFI robust = .890, TLI robust = .884, RMSEA robust = .054[0.53, 0.55], substantially improved model fit relative to the one single second-order factor model in particular, Δχ²(3) = 946 (p < .001), ΔCFI robust = .021; ΔTLI robust = .022 ΔRMSEA robust = .005, and to a slighter extent relative to the model with two second-order factors representing conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial content, Δχ²(2) = 259 (p < .001), ΔCFI robust = .008; ΔRMSEA robust = .002. However, model fit was still subpar in the absolute sense (in terms of incremental fit indices), as could be expected based on the latent correlations.

Systematic Method Covariance

Correlations between the marker variable and index scores for the substantive factors were close to zero and non-significant in most cases, despite the large sample size (average absolute correlation across all factors: r s = .03). Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents). These results suggest that the amount of systematic method covariance related to response biases in the data was negligible overall relative to the strong covariances between the substantive factors of interest.

Discussion

The results were once again mostly supportive of the weak generality hypothesis, with substantial correlations between most primary factors. There was, however, greater variation in the magnitude of the latent correlations in this study (e.g., around a fourth of them were weak), and the strong generality hypothesis was not supported at all, as the ECV indicated that the general factor accounted for less than half of the common variance among latent factors, which is substantially below what could reasonably be expected given a dominant general factor. Furthermore, this study yielded clear evidence for a meaningful distinction between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial forms of misinformation susceptibility, with significant improvements in model fit when these were split up into separate second-order factors rather than lumped together. Interestingly, the improvement in model fit was even larger when left-wing, ideologically neutral, and right-wing forms of misinformation were represented by separate second-order factors, suggesting that ideological tilt plays a key role in what kinds of misinformation people endorse.

There were generally stronger correlations between the conspiratorial factors than between those without conspiratorial content, suggesting more of a common core for these, as might be expected. In fact, conspiracy mentality overlapped with conspiracy theories regarding sham democracy to such a degree that we had to collapse the two factors into a general conspiracist ideation factor for the models to converge. This was plausibly because both scales contained items expressing conspiracist narratives about the political system.

Furthermore, the latent correlations between this factor and belief in other more specific conspiracy theories were consistently very strong, consistent with the notion that it captured general ingredients of conspiratorial thinking, such as anti-authority or anti-establishment stances (Imhoff, 2024).

There was one notable exception, where an equally strong correlation emerged between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial contents: belief in conspiracies about a coverup of extraterrestrial activity had a very strong latent correlation with paranormal beliefs-stronger than with any of its conspiratorial siblings, in fact-and strong correlations also with belief in astrology and pseudoscience. These results point to a possible common core of mystical, magical, or new age thinking influencing misinformation susceptibility irrespective of conspiratorial content. At the same time, belief in pseudoscience loaded much higher on the aggregated second-order factor than other non-conspiratorial factors did-and in fact higher than most of the conspiratorial ones as well-suggesting that this particular scale captured misinformation susceptibility more broadly, beyond new age thinking.

Another noteworthy finding is that there were stronger and more consistent correlations between factors representing susceptibility to misinformation with a right-wing ideological tilt (i.e., global warming denial and conspiracy theories about liberal elites) than among those with a left-wing tilt. In fact, IQ-denial and blank slateism, which were assumed to represent left-wing misinformation, exhibited the most uniqueness out of all the scales.

Data Quality

The inclusion of marker variables allowed us to assess the potential influence of response style biases inflating correlations. Pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity stood out in terms of having a slightly higher correlation with the marker variable compared to other factors, suggesting that there may have been a small degree of response style bias affecting this measure more than the others. A possible reason could be that the measurement places a higher cognitive demand on participants, resulting in participants defaulting to a response style more agnostic of item content. At the same time, the correlations between the substantive factors and the marker variable were negligible overall, particularly compared to the very strong covariation between the substantive factors, suggesting that systematic method variance had little effect on the factor structure.

The discrepancies in the strength of results across the two studies may have been, at least partly, the result of poorer data quality in Study 1, with more careless responding and response styles biases inflating the latent correlations. While we did not formally test whether the latent correlations were indeed more inflated by systematic method covariance in Study 1, we see no clear theoretical reason that various forms of misinformation susceptibility should be substantially less differentiated in a Swedish population than in a British one. In Study 2, not only were the overall correlations among measures in the data lower, but they were also more systematically in line with theoretical expectations. For instance, in Study 1, pseudoprofound bullshit receptivity showed latent correlations with other factors roughly comparable to those of the other variables, while in Study 2, it had substantially lower correlations with the other aspects of misinformation receptivity. The Study 2 result is more in line with expectations provided both that pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity constitutes a qualitatively different kind of misinformation (i.e., nonsense without propositional content), measured with different response anchors and a different set of instructions (i.e., about rating the profundity of a statement rather than its truth). Based on this alone, one would expect careful and conscientious respondents to differ more in their inclinations to score a certain way on bullshit, as was the case in study 2.

General Discussion

Despite an increased interest in the psychology of misinformation susceptibility, researchers have paid little attention to whether it reflects a general tendency that cuts across domains or a set of largely distinct, domain-specific tendencies. As a result, potential commonalities across categories of misinformation have been underexplored, leaving the literature fragmented and disorganized. Although several studies have shown correlations across different kinds of misinformation (Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bensley et al., 2020 Bensley et al., , 2022;; Lobato et al., 2014; van Prooijen et al., 2018), the dimensionality across measures had not previously been rigorously examined. In the current research, we therefore investigated the covariance structure of misinformation susceptibility using a large battery of measures covering belief in unwarranted conspiracy theories, antiscientific and pseudoscientific statements, and pseudo-profound bullshit in two large samples of Swedish and British adults.

The Generality Hypothesis

The findings generally provide evidence for weak generality (Bensley et al., 2020 (Bensley et al., , 2022;; Lobato et al., 2014), showing a pattern of substantial and significant correlations across measures, including some of which are clearly distinct in content a priori (e.g., belief in pseudoscience, unwarranted conspiracy theories, and pseudo-profound bullshit). Although the correlations were slightly lower in Study 2, most of them remained highly significant and of substantial magnitude in the ESEM robustness analyses using target rotation in both studies.

At the same time, the findings do not clearly support strong generality-that is, a general or common factor did not adequately account for the systematic covariance across the variety of measures. There was some weak or partial support for strong generality in Study 1, as indicated by acceptable model fit based on absolute fit indices (RMSEA and SRMR) for the bifactor model. However, the bifactor model still fit substantially worse than the correlated factors model even in Study 1, despite the generally high fitting propensity of bifactor models noted in the literature (e.g., Greene et al., 2019). Moreover, both SRMR and RMSEA tend to give overly optimistic fit estimates in models with many degrees of freedom and large sample sizes (Kenny et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2018). On the other hand, CFI has a general tendency to display worse fit for models with many indicators (Kenny & McCoach, 2003). In short, attempting to use any one-size-fits-all cut-off criteria to judge model fit is an endeavour fraught with perils and surrounded by controversy (e.g., Bazzoli, 2024; Edwards, 2013; Hancock & Mueller, 2011; Marsh et al., 2004; McNeish & Manapat, 2024; McNeish et al., 2018; Nguyen, 2025; Preacher, 2006; Shi et al., 2018).

Furthermore, while ECV indicated that roughly half of the common variance among latent factors (61% in Study 1; 47% in Study 2) was attributable to the general factor, this is still below the mean ECV of the pool of bifactor models examined in Rodriguez et al. (2016) and considerably short of the .7-.8 range that would be expected with a dominant general factor. Furthermore, given the probable presence of many unmodeled small yet non-zero cross-loadings in the bifactor models and the far from ideal model fit of these models, the ECVs reported are likely, if anything, overestimating the strength of a general factor (Reise, 2012), as the omitted crossloadings end up being absorbed by the general factor. The strong generality hypothesis can therefore be considered rejected.

While Smallpage et al. (2023) provided a test of a hierarchical structure of misinformation (a second-order factor explained the covariation between conspiracy mentality, pseudoscientific, and paranormal beliefs), the model they tested contained three first-order factors, making it hard to differentiate from a correlated factors model.

Furthermore, as noted in the literature (e.g., Savalei, 2018; Xia & Yang, 2019), fit evaluation using weighted least squares based estimators can be problematic to evaluate using traditional, ML-based points of reference. Using a large number of indicators and first-order factors along with MLR-estimation made it possible for us to test and evaluate the strong generality hypothesis more directly.

Do these results imply that it would be misguided to calculate a general score for misinformation susceptibility? From a pragmatic viewpoint, interpretable aggregated scores could be provided by hierarchical measurement models, absent strict unidimensionality (Yang & Green, 2015). Indeed, not even IQ scores are fully unidimensional, representing domainspecific cognitive skills and abilities beyond general intelligence (g), but this does not necessarily detract from the usefulness of the g-factor model (Colom et al., 2002). However, misinformation susceptibility fell substantially below a priori thresholds in terms of ECV in the current studies. Furthermore, while misinformation susceptibility may share similarities with broad trait domains (e.g., extraversion or neuroticism) in terms of its structure, it is likely more difficult to capture with a single generic hierarchical model. This is because misinformation is a broad theoretical concept covering a vast universe of exemplars that is difficult (if not impossible) to pin down in its entirety, and there are likely multiple ways to partition it into facets depending on which specific exemplars are included in any given study.

In these respects, misinformation susceptibility may be more similar to the concept of political ideology. Although we know today that political ideology is not reducible to a single left-right dimension, and there are a multitude of more fine-grained models of ideology (Feldman & Johnston, 2014; Nilsson et al., 2020; Schwartz et al., 2010), the left-right dimension remains widely treated as a practically useful, course-grained model of general ideology (Kteily & Brandt, 2024). Analogously, it may be possible to assess general aspects of misinformation susceptibility, such as a general tendency to believe in unwarranted conspiracy theories, although we need to keep in mind that such models are unlikely to adequately capture the entire domain.

Other Sources of Covariation

Conspiratorial Content. Beyond generalities across all categories of misinformation, another source of covariation in the data was whether the misinformation represented conspiratorial content or not. The results show a high degree of generality across different kinds of conspiratorial beliefs, albeit with some additional variation attributable to ideological tilt. A model that divided the initial second-order factor up into two correlated second-order factors, representing conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial content, respectively, yielded a considerable improvement in model fit in Study 2. Although the change in model fit was low in Study 1 in particular, and the two second-order factors remained very strongly correlated even in Study 2, these results should be interpreted with caution, as it is highly likely given the size of the model that latent correlations and ostensible overlap between factors were likely considerably inflated by the sheer amount of cross-loadings fixed to zero. Taken together, the results suggest that there is a distinct dimension of susceptibility to unwarranted conspiracy theories-that is, some people are more susceptible to misinformation when it is framed in terms of a conspiratorial narrative. This is likely one of the drivers of the lack of strong generality in the data.

The latent correlations suggest that there was more of a common core across the measures with conspiratorial content. This is not surprising, as the non-conspiratorial measures were grouped together based on what they are not, rather than what they have in common. Unlike the conspiratorial content, they did not align with a common worldview.

Ideological Content.

Analyses taking the ideological tilt of the misinformation into consideration even more clearly demonstrate that the congruence between the misinformation and people's worldviews was a source of covariation in the data. A second-order model where we divided up the constructs according to their a priori ideological tilt (right-wing, neutral, and left-wing) resulted in substantially improved model fit compared to the other secondorder models for both studies, suggesting that ideological alignment was a contributing factor.

Additionally, these results are consistent with the notion that specific conspiracy theories are often contaminated by ideological content (Imhoff et al., 2022).

Interestingly, there was a clearer common core across the right-wing forms of misinformation than the left-wing or neutral ones. There are several possible explanations for this asymmetry. First, it might arise due to differences in misinformation susceptibility between ideological groups. Insofar as social conservatives are more epistemically vulnerable on average (e.g., Nilsson et al., 2024; Smallpage et al., 2023), their responses may to a greater extent drive correlations between the factors, resulting in higher correlations between measures with conservative content. Second, the asymmetry in question may be rooted in differential exposure. Insofar as misinformation is currently more often spread on the political right than on the left (Garrett & Bond, 2021), right-wingers should be more likely to adopt an entire "package" of misinformed beliefs from elite political discourse and ingroup authorities.

Third, it may be that the right-wing forms of misinformation, such as global warming denial and conspiracy theories about liberal elites, in themselves represent more of a coherent ideological package, whereas some forms of misinformation that we assumed would be characteristic of the left, such as IQ-denial and blank slateism, are less integrated in contemporary left-wing ideological discourse. A different selection of scales might have resulted in higher correlations between left-leaning contents.

Science-Related Content. Another potential source of covariation between measures is the extent to which they capture familiarity with scientific results or intellectual discourse. In an exploratory factor analysis of unfounded beliefs, Bensley et al. (2020) found distinct (but strongly correlated) factors representing conspiracy-and science-related content.

In the current research, IQ-denial and blank slateism were relatively unique compared to other forms of misinformation receptivity. Although these are commonly referred to as examples of science-related misinformation on the left (e.g., Lewandowsky & Oberauer, 2016), those exposed to it may in reality constitute a small minority (i.e., individuals in particular intellectual circles or educational milieus), compared to, for example, those exposed to misinformation about global warming. Analogously, Nilsson et al. (2024) found that although individuals with progressive values were more susceptible to pseudo-profound bullshit with left-wing jargon, they were not more susceptible to postmodern bullshit, plausibly reflecting low familiarity with postmodernism among the general public.

Alternatively, it could be that IQ-denial and blank slateism are perceived as more plausible and intuitively defensible for many who would otherwise correctly identify other forms of science-related misinformation, because environmental determinism used to be a respected account in the nature-nurture debate only decades ago (Pinker, 2006; Plomin et al., 1994). Given that the epistemic warrant for these beliefs has changed relatively recently, whether people endorse them may reflect their broader worldviews more than a domainindependent susceptibility to science-related misinformation.

Mystical Content.

Another theoretically meaningful finding was that there were particularly strong correlations between factors representing belief in conspiracy theories about a coverup of extraterrestrial activity, paranormal phenomena, and astrology. What these have in common is a belief in unobservable, mystical entities, such as ghosts, spirits, and extraterrestrials, and mystical or magical forms of causation that are not consistent with a scientific worldview, including effects of celestial bodies on personality and the possibility of interacting with the dead. Therefore, the results suggest that a mystical worldview constitutes an additional source of variation in misinformation susceptibility, beyond generalities, conspiratorial content, ideology, and science knowledge.

Although belief in pseudoscience correlated strongly with these types of misinformation susceptibility, it also correlated strongly with measures capturing, for example, other types of conspiratorial thinking. This is likely because this measure covered a multitude of pseudoscientific ideas, some of which are more aligned with mysticism, such as the law of attraction, and some of which are more aligned with general or science-related conspiratorial narratives without entailing a mystical worldview, such as anti-vaccination discourse.

Limitations and Future Directions

One potential cause for concern is the misfit of the second-order models, according to the incremental fit indices. Given the size of these models and the mediocre model fit, there is cause for concern that model misspecification may be inflating parameter estimates (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009; Maydeu-Olivares, 2017). Furthermore, the standard errors associated with the factor loadings were generally larger than what might be expected given our sample size. This may suggest some added degree of instability (uncertainty) in our estimates. However, this concern may be alleviated to some extent by the large sample size of both of our studies, meaning that the absolute sizes of the standard errors are still relatively small.

Another limitation is that we did not investigate the underlying psychological factors that drive the structure of misinformation susceptibility. Some factors, such as higher intuitive and subjectivist thinking, and lower analytical and actively open-minded thinking, plausibly yield higher general misinformation susceptibility across domains (e.g., Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bensley et al., 2022; Pennycook et al., 2015; Ståhl & van Prooijen, 2018; Torres et al., 2023).

Others may have more local effects. For example, distrust in experts may yield higher susceptibility specifically to misinformation with a conspiratorial or science-related component, at least in cultures that value science (Bensley et al., 2022), but it should be less relevant to bullshit receptivity. Similarly, political partisanship or extremism, scientific knowledge, and religiosity may matter particularly for misinformation with ideologically congruent, science-related, or mystical components, respectively (e.g., Lindeman & Aarnio, 2006; Washburn & Skitka, 2018). Furthermore, hypersensitive detection of agency and purpose in the material world may particularly predict susceptibility to conspiracy theories, paranormal beliefs, and some forms of pseudoscience (e.g., Boudry et al., 2015; Douglas et al., 2016), rather than other forms of science misinformation or bullshit; and threat sensitivity may predict receptivity to misinformation with conspiratorial or in other ways threat-evoking content (Van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018). Further research is needed to rigorously test which explanations hold up across which forms of misinformation.

Future studies that investigate multiple potential sources of systematic covariation beyond a general misinformation susceptibility (e.g., conspiracy theories, mysticism, essentialism, trust in science, knowledge about science, political ideology), should consider including marker variables or other approaches to assess presence of systematic method covariance in the data.

Limitations on Generalisability

Although we collected data from two countries with a large and diverse battery of measures, the extent to which the conclusions generalize to other measures and countries is unknown. A potential complication is that misinformation susceptibility may be contingent upon the information environment people are immersed in, which varies across cultures and shifts over time. While we anticipate that the general categories recur universally (e.g., conspiratorial, ideological, science-related, and mystical content), the specific exemplars that are most relevant within a given context may vary. Therefore, it may be difficult to create a single standardized measurement that holds across time and place. Further research is thus needed to develop measurements calibrated to various settings, while assessing the stability of the general conceptual structure. To this end, we recommend that researchers focus on general types of misinformation (e.g., pseudoscience, unwarranted conspiracy theories, and pseudoprofound bullshit) rather than specific "fake news" stories, which go out of date quickly and generalize poorly across populations. Furthermore, it may be worthwhile to investigate whether the structure of misinformation susceptibility is more constrained by elite discourse and propaganda in autocratic regimes than in democracies (Dunwoody et al., 2022).

Additionally, future studies should investigate whether conspiracy theories are less integrated into the misinformation network in societies with higher levels or political and institutional corruption, where at least some of them may have higher epistemic warrant (Alper & Imhoff, 2022). This would shed further light on the degree to which the associations are driven by the implausibility of the contents rather than the conspiratorial narratives per se (Frenken et al., 2025).

Conclusions

The findings across two studies suggest that there is a clear degree of generality across different aspects of misinformation susceptibility, as evidenced by generally substantial and significant latent correlations across measures (i.e., generality in the weaker sense). This generality is not strong enough to be adequately captured by a general factor (i.e., generality in the stronger sense), however, suggesting that the type and content of the misinformationfor example, whether it incorporates a conspiratorial or ideological narrative or elements of mysticism, magical thinking, or science denial-still plays a considerable role. These findings suggest that it is advantageous to divide misinformation susceptibility into several interrelated domains rather than treating it as a single homogeneous dimension.
